key_terms.meaning: Binary data changes the carrier amplitude: s(t)=A b(t) cos(2πf_c t), with b(t)=1 for bit 1 and 0 for bit 0.
Bit 0 and bit 1 use carriers f0 and f1: s_i(t)=A cos(2πf_i t), i=0,1.
Filter h(t)=s(T_b−t) maximizes output SNR at sampling time T_b for a known pulse s(t).
Binary phase-shift keying sends s(t)=A cos(2πf_c t+πb), b∈{0,1}, so the two signals are antipodal.
Q(x)=P(Z>x) for standard normal Z; binary antipodal error is P_b=Q(√(2E_b/N0)), with E_b bit energy and N0 one-sided noise density.
Differential phase-shift keying encodes each bit as a phase change from the previous symbol, so absolute carrier phase is not needed.
Detection without a recovered carrier phase, using envelope or square-law detectors; used for FSK and DPSK.
Quadrature phase-shift keying maps two bits to one of four phases, giving two bits per symbol.
M-ary PSK uses M=2^k phases to send k bits per symbol; larger M reduces spacing for the same power.
M-ary FSK uses M orthogonal tones, one per symbol; bandwidth grows with M while power efficiency can improve.
Quadrature amplitude modulation sets independent I and Q amplitudes: s(t)=I cos(2πf_c t)−Q sin(2πf_c t).
Minimum-shift keying is continuous-phase FSK with modulation index h=0.5, so tones are separated by 1/(2T_b).
Gaussian minimum-shift keying passes the data through a Gaussian low-pass filter before MSK, shrinking spectrum and adding controlled ISI.
A plot of signal vectors in an orthonormal basis; distances set error probability and number of points sets bits per symbol.
The smallest Euclidean distance between two constellation points; larger d_min gives lower error probability at fixed noise.
η=R_b/B bits/s/Hz, where R_b is bit rate and B is occupied bandwidth.
Direct-sequence spread spectrum multiplies the data by a fast pseudorandom chip code, spreading it over a wide band.
Frequency-hopping spread spectrum changes the carrier frequency in a pseudorandom pattern, one hop per dwell interval.
Orthogonal frequency-division multiplexing sends N low-rate subcarriers spaced Δf=1/T_u and implemented by IFFT/FFT.
A copy of the end of each OFDM symbol placed at its start; it absorbs delay spread if longer than the channel memory.

takeaways: ASK and FSK map bits to amplitude or frequency; coherent detection with matched filters or correlators needs carrier phase, while non-coherent detection avoids it.
BPSK is the best binary scheme in AWGN because antipodal signals have the largest distance for fixed bit energy, with P_b=Q(√(2E_b/N0)).
DPSK trades a small error penalty for no absolute phase recovery, which helps when carrier phase wanders.
QPSK sends two bits per symbol and, with Gray coding, has the same bit error probability as BPSK at the same E_b/N0.
MFSK and QAM offer opposite trade-offs: MFSK spends bandwidth to gain power efficiency, while QAM spends power to gain bandwidth efficiency.
MSK keeps phase continuous and the envelope constant; GMSK filters data to reduce out-of-band spectrum at the cost of ISI.
Constellation minimum distance controls error probability, while constellation size controls bits per symbol and bandwidth efficiency.
DSSS and FHSS spread a signal with a pseudorandom code to resist interference, and OFDM turns a frequency-selective channel into parallel flat subchannels using IFFT/FFT and a cyclic prefix.
bank_note: Long answers usually require signal-space diagrams, generation and detection block diagrams, error-probability expressions, and explicit bandwidth-versus-power comparisons across schemes.

bank.q: Explain binary ASK and binary FSK generation and coherent detection with block diagrams. State the decision rule and the role of the matched filter.
outline: ASK modulator multiplies the carrier by unipolar data; FSK modulator selects f0 or f1.
Coherent receiver multiplies by a reference carrier or tone and integrates over T_b.
Matched filter with impulse response s(T_b−t) maximizes sampled SNR.
Decision threshold at the midpoint; for orthogonal FSK compare correlator outputs.
Draw signal-space diagrams for ASK and FSK.

bank.q: Define BPSK. Draw its signal-space diagram and derive P_b=Q(√(2E_b/N0)) for an AWGN channel.
outline: BPSK waveform s(t)=A cos(2πf_c t+πb), b∈{0,1}.
Two antipodal points at ±√E_b on one signal-space axis.
Generation by balanced modulator or phase selector.
Coherent detector with carrier recovery and sign decision.
Noise variance N0/2 leads to P_b=Q(√(2E_b/N0)).

bank.q: Compare coherent BFSK, non-coherent BFSK, and DPSK detection. What carrier-phase information does each need?
outline: Coherent BFSK uses two reference tones and needs carrier phase.
Non-coherent BFSK uses envelope or square-law detectors and needs no phase.
DPSK compares the current symbol phase with the previous symbol phase.
Non-coherent FSK and DPSK pay an error-probability penalty.
Use these schemes when phase recovery is difficult.

bank.q: Describe QPSK generation and detection. Why does Gray-coded QPSK have the same bit error probability as BPSK at the same E_b/N0?
outline: QPSK maps two bits to I and Q signs: s(t)=I cos(2πf_c t)−Q sin(2πf_c t).
Generation uses serial-to-parallel conversion, polar NRZ, and a quadrature modulator.
Detection uses two coherent correlators for I and Q.
Gray mapping makes adjacent phases differ by one bit.
Gray-coded QPSK BER equals BPSK BER at the same E_b/N0.

bank.q: An ASK system uses on-off keying with bit rate 10 kbit/s and carrier 100 kHz. Sketch the modulator and coherent receiver, and explain threshold setting in noise.
outline: On-off keying sends s(t)=A cos(2πf_c t) for bit 1 and zero for bit 0.
T_b=100 μs; carrier frequency is 100 kHz.
Coherent receiver multiplies, integrates over T_b, and samples.
Threshold is half the noiseless peak; noise causes errors.
Main-lobe null-to-null bandwidth is about 2R_b=20 kHz.

bank.q: A BPSK link has E_b/N0=8 dB. Find P_b using Q(√(2E_b/N0)) and explain how the result changes if the signal is turned off for bit 0 (OOK).
outline: 8 dB gives E_b/N0=6.31 in linear scale.
BPSK uses antipodal signals.
OOK with the same average bit energy needs about 3 dB more E_b/N0 for the same P_b.

bank.q: Design a 16-QAM constellation with Gray mapping. Compute bits per symbol, relative bandwidth efficiency, and compare minimum distance with 16-PSK at the same average symbol energy.
outline: 16-QAM sends log2 16=4 bits per symbol.
Use a 4×4 grid with I and Q levels ±1 and ±3.
Gray mapping reduces bit errors per symbol error.
At the same average symbol energy, 16-QAM has larger minimum distance than 16-PSK.
Ideal bandwidth efficiency is about 4 bits/s/Hz for Nyquist signalling.

bank.q: An OFDM system has 64 subcarriers and useful symbol time 3.2 μs. Find subcarrier spacing and choose a cyclic prefix for a channel delay spread of 0.8 μs. Explain the choice.
outline: Subcarrier spacing Δf=1/T_u=1/(3.2 μs)=312.5 kHz.
Cyclic prefix length must exceed 0.8 μs; choose 0.8–1.0 μs with margin.
Cyclic prefix prevents inter-block interference.
Overhead is T_cp/(T_u+T_cp); with 0.8 μs it is 20%.
Longer prefix gives more protection but lower efficiency.

bank.q: A DSSS system uses 127 chips per bit and BPSK chips. Find processing gain in dB and explain how it helps against a narrowband interferer.
outline: Processing gain G_p=10 log10(127)=21.0 dB.
DSSS spreads the data over a wide band.
Despreading adds the desired signal coherently.
A narrowband interferer is spread and then filtered.
Jamming margin and near-far effects limit practical gain.

bank.q: Compare BPSK, QPSK, 16-PSK, and 16-QAM at equal average bit energy. Discuss error probability, spectrum, and suitability for a power-limited versus bandwidth-limited link.
outline: At equal E_b/N0, BPSK and Gray QPSK have the same BER.
16-PSK has smaller angular spacing than 16-QAM at equal average energy.
Bandwidth efficiency rises with constellation size.
Power efficiency falls as minimum distance shrinks.
Power-limited links favour BPSK/QPSK; bandwidth-limited links favour QAM.

bank.q: Explain why MSK has constant envelope and continuous phase, and evaluate the GMSK filter trade-off between spectral containment and ISI in a nonlinear link.
outline: MSK is CPFSK with h=0.5 and phase continuity.
Tone separation 1/(2T_b) gives orthogonal signalling.
Constant envelope suits nonlinear amplifiers.
GMSK Gaussian filter reduces spectral sidelobes.
Filtering adds ISI; BT product trades spectrum against eye closure.

bank.q: A frequency-selective channel has delay spread comparable to the symbol time. Compare a single-carrier QAM link with an OFDM link using a cyclic prefix; discuss equalization, PAPR, and synchronization.
outline: Single-carrier QAM suffers ISI and needs an equalizer.
OFDM converts the channel into flat subcarriers with one-tap equalizers.
Cyclic prefix longer than delay spread removes inter-block interference.
OFDM has high PAPR and is sensitive to frequency and timing errors.
Compare complexity, spectral efficiency, and adaptive loading.

bank.q: Compare DSSS and FHSS for interference rejection and multiple access. Include processing gain, chip rate, hopping rate, and near-far issues.
outline: DSSS uses a fast chip code and has processing gain.
FHSS hops the carrier and resists partial-band interference.
DSSS supports CDMA by code separation.
FHSS supports multiple access by hop patterns.
Near-far problems are severe in DSSS; synchronization is critical in both.

bank.q: Evaluate the statement: Higher-order QAM always improves performance because it sends more bits per symbol. Use constellation distance and bandwidth efficiency in your answer.
outline: Higher-order QAM raises bits per symbol and bandwidth efficiency.
At fixed average power, constellation points crowd and d_min falls.
Error probability rises unless SNR is increased.
Distinguish bandwidth-limited from power-limited operation.
Practical limits include linearity, PAPR, phase noise, and converter resolution.

glossary.def: A signal whose spectrum is centered on a nonzero carrier frequency f_c.
A signal whose spectrum is centered at zero frequency.
A sinusoidal wave at f_c that carries data by amplitude, phase, or frequency changes.
One transmitted waveform chosen from a finite set; it may carry one or more bits.
A binary digit, 0 or 1.
Additive white Gaussian noise, a model with constant power spectral density N0/2 over all frequencies.
Detection that uses a locally recovered carrier with known phase and frequency.
Detection that does not need the absolute carrier phase, often using envelope or square-law detection.
A linear filter matched to the pulse shape that maximizes sampled SNR in AWGN.
A receiver that multiplies the received signal by a reference waveform and integrates over the symbol interval.
A circuit that extracts the slowly varying amplitude of a bandpass signal, used in non-coherent ASK and FSK.
Differential phase-shift keying, where information is carried by phase changes between successive symbols.
A bit mapping in which adjacent constellation points differ by one bit, reducing bit errors per symbol error.
The set of signal vectors plotted in an orthonormal signal space.
Signals whose inner product is zero over the symbol interval; they do not interfere in an ideal correlator.
Ratio of signal power to noise power, often expressed per bit as E_b/N0.
Bit energy divided by one-sided noise power spectral density; a standard power-efficiency measure.
In CPFSK, h=2Δf T_b, where Δf is frequency deviation and T_b is bit duration; MSK uses h=0.5.
One pulse of a pseudorandom spreading code; chip rate is usually much larger than bit rate.
The ratio of spread bandwidth to data bandwidth, often 10 log10(chips per bit) dB.
Intersymbol interference, the overlap of one symbol pulse with neighbouring symbols after a band-limited channel.
The time spread between the earliest and latest significant multipath arrivals.
The frequency range over which the channel response is approximately flat.
One of many narrowband carriers in OFDM or multicarrier modulation.
A guard interval made by copying the tail of an OFDM symbol to its start to prevent inter-block interference.
Peak-to-average power ratio, a measure of waveform peaks relative to average power.
